headline:
Feasts & Celebrations;
Collecting the Old and . . . the New
abstract: Whether it is a reproduction of a Chinese export porcelain plate that was used in an English castle in the 1800's, or a silver teapot that could have been your great-grandmother's, the look of the past is appearing more often on tabletops today. Antique dealers and flea markets sell a wide range of period designs, which are being collected to be used and not just displayed. And, increasingly, sources from burgeoning museum mail-order businesses to manufacturers such as Minton and Towle are offering reproductions and heirloom-inspired examples. Many of the new wares will cost less than their older counterparts, but not necessarily -- the vagaries of pricing at antiques and flea markets means that a dedicated collector can often find pieces for modest expense. In either case, the thing to remember is that collecting does not need to be done all at once; rather, it is an investment preferably enjoyed over a period of years.

headline: In the Heartland Of Old Germany
abstract:
TRAVELING today in what was until recently the German Democratic Republic is an experience at once depressing and fascinating. Depressing, because of the dereliction of the towns, the mood of dazed anxiety and the poor state of tourist services, bureaucratic and not very customer-friendly. Fascinating, because of the bizarre outward symptoms of current revolutionary change (and resistance to it), and the historic and cultural riches of the area from Dresden to Weimar and Eisenach that was the very heartland of the glorious pre-World War I German tradition, so closely linked with Bach, Luther, Goethe, Wagner and others.

Take Leipzig, population 560,000, second city of the former East Germany. It was long a major center of music, literature and publishing, with a great trade fair that still exists. But the surrounding heavy industry, notably the chemical works at Bitterfeld, were allowed by the old regime to grow into such a cesspool of pollution that Leipzig's air is chokingly foul. In the past the city was also exploited for the benefit of East Berlin, deprived of its resources, crippled by neglect; the fierce local resentments against this help to explain why last fall's revolution started there, with the Monday meetings in the Nikolaikirche and the mass rallies on the Karl Marx Platz.

headline: Interior Motives
abstract:
Miss Page Rense
Architectural Digest
Los Angeles, Calif.
Dear Miss Rense:

Although I could never afford the lifestyle of the people who live in the sumptuous homes you show, I am an avid fan of your fabulous magazine. I especially like to see how celebrities live and wonder which issue I should buy to get a look at Candy and Aaron Spelling's quintessential new Hollywood home, built with profits from "Dynasty" and "Love Boat." I read in a gossip column that their mansion is bigger than the White House, cost over $50 million and has its own bowling alley. 

Hoping to hear from you soon.
 A Decorating Fan.
Dear Fan,

Your letter is deeply appreciated, since every genuine letter to the editor we receive means my hard-working staff has one less to create for our Letters column.

It is gratifying to learn that you enjoy our celebrity features, since, believe me, it is not easy finding well-known people whose taste lives up to our standards.

There is a common misconception that Architectural Digest glorifies conspicuous consumption, which couldn't be farther from the truth. In my two decades here, we have occasionally published some grand houses, but our motto for the 90's is, Bigger Isn't Better, except in circulation, advertising and miscellaneous revenues.

Regarding the Spelling house, at present we have no plans to publish it -- which has nothing to do with my disdain for bowling.

As a consolation, I am enclosing some tips from a book I'm thinking of writing next weekend (it will be my 15th, if my assistant has counted correctly) . It will be called "You Don't Say: Paige Rense's Guide to Taboo Celebrity House Talk."

 -- Don't say "home," say "house."

-- Don't use trite words like "lifestyle," "sumptuous," "fabulous" or "quintessential."

 -- Always spell Paige with an i.

 Cordially,
 Paige Rense, editor in chief

It's easy to parody Paige Rense -- to make fun of her legendary no-nos, her concocted reader letters, her magazine's pretentious tone and extravagant taste, and the idea of one person's passing judgment on thousands of houses every year -- particularly a woman who didn't know Gaudi from gaudy when she started. But you can't underestimate her accomplishments. In 19 years at the helm of Architectural Digest, with meager magazine experience and an initial operating budget that wasn't much larger than one competitor's annual taxi allotment, Rense has turned a marginal building-trades magazine published by Knapp Communications into a top-of-the-line voyeur's bible -- the National Geographic of interior design, art and antiques. Between 1971 and 1989, she has taken circulation from 50,000 to 625,000, and advertising revenues from less than $1 million to $46 million. And all this in a magazine backwater called Los Angeles.

Today Architectural Digest stands supreme among the "shelter magazines" -- the thick and glossy periodicals devoted to decorating and home furnishings, a multibillion-dollar industry in the United States. Rense earns a salary estimated at about $600,000 -- a queen's ransom in the magazine world. Exposure in AD has become so important to decorators that she has seen some completed jobs before the client has. Decorators the world over take a rejection of their work by Rense as the ultimate snub ("a maniac" one of them called her after finding himself left out of "The AD 100," the magazine's recent issue devoted to the top 100 designers whose work has appeared in its pages). Yet none dare cross her, for fear of winding up in Rolodex limbo. ("Strike him off all of our lists now!" she has ruled.) 

The magazine casts a mesmerizing spell over its readers. It isn't hip like Metropolitan Home (circulation 701,000), with its witty mix of basic-Biedermeier and Mies-to-go; it isn't "how-to" like House Beautiful (circulation, 932,000); it wouldn't be caught dead showing $500,000 his-and-her kitchens or trendy lofts like the young-but-rich HG (circulation, 619,900), and it has none of the torn curtains or socks under the bed in the throwaway-chic World of Interiors (circulation, 73,000).

No, Architectural Digest -- "The International Magazine of Fine Interior Design" -- is one continuous house tour, where glitz and refinement cohabit happily. Cher's house -- or houses (AD has printed four of them so far) -- is just as welcome as Baron Thyssen-Bornemisza's private museum and Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother's house at Sandringham (coming in AD in January).

The magazine really came into its own in the early 1980's, when more-is-more began to replace less-is-more as a (pardon the word) lifestyle credo. "Money was suddenly beautiful, and the Digest was the only upscale design magazine," observes Steven Cohn of Media Industry Newsletter.

It wasn't long before less pricey shelter magazines moved into the same "affluential" (a Rense coinage) neighborhood, but Digest has remained in a class by itself.

"Pretentious" is the word some use to describe Rense's drawing-room-drama approach, especially her appetite for opulence in present-day interior decoration. "It's like a Potemkin village," says Ira Levy, senior vice-president for creative corporate development at Estee Lauder. "Everything is too perfect."

But love the magazine -- or love to dish it -- AD is a must read. "It's glued to everyone's coffee table," says Mario Buatta, the decorator, who has had his share of glory in it. "My clients treasure it," says Patricia Crane, a Bryn Mawr, Pa., designer whose work has never appeared in Digest. "This is success," she adds with a sniff, "what they aspire to." 

 "Aspire" doesn't begin to cover it. According to one story, which may even be true, a Beverly Hills woman on her deathbed received a call from her daughter, who said she'd be delayed coming over because Architectural Digest was photographing her house. In that case, said the mother. "Don't worry about me. Take your time." 

THE SIGN ON THE wooden door that leads into Architectural Digest's viewing room warns away unauthorized personnel with a stern "Do Not Enter." They don't. Here, 30 floors above Wilshire Boulevard, is the heart of the AD dream machine. File cabinets filled with photos line the walls and divide the room; along one wall runs a deep shelf holding a row of light boxes. Three to four times a month, the fate of thousands of designers, photographers and houses is decided. There is no jury, just the judge -- Paige Rense, who has seen it all.

At the appointed hour Rense sweeps in with a "Hi, darlin' " for her art director, Thomas Sullivan. The greeting reflects the "New West" Rense: she just bought land in Jackson Hole, Wyo., and she's negotiating to buy a house in Santa Fe, N.M., and these days she favors denim cowgirl skirts, boots and a slow drawl.

Her looks are deceiving. Some days she seems as plain as a movie star before breakfast; large glasses disguise a hint of sadness in her eyes. But then suddenly, for an audience, for a camera, for a decorator passing through "on his way to Pittsburgh," she lights up -- and 

heeeeeeere's 

Paige: extremely photogenic, she has large blue eyes that never blink at a strobe flash, a pug nose, a vivacious Ginger Rogers smile, and a souffle of blond frosted hair.

Like women of her generation who found it smart to play dumb (Rense admits to 57 but is actually 61), she often lapses into a cute little-girl's voice. She talks softly and lets deputies carry the big stick. Constantly called on to judge the creative efforts of others, she has developed a reassuring ooh-and-aah delivery of "Oh, how wonderful," "Oh, how marvelous." When she really likes something, though, she'll bang both hands on the nearest surface, palms down, and exclaim, "Great!"

Right now, the pictures are laid out on the light boxes for Rense's review. Her back slightly curved from years of hunching over these viewing boxes, she works her way quickly from left to right, as her art director, "photographer liaison" (AD has no photo editor) and assistants stand by quietly noting her decisions. Then she starts over, moving rightward, until the current backlog is disposed of -- one way or another. The little-girl voice is never used here. And her decision is final. The absence of give and take is awesome. 

The staff can't predict what she'll like. Using her legendary intuition, she calculates at a glance the uniqueness of the design, the impact of the photographs, the prominence of the resident, the importance of the designer -- and whir, whir, click, click -- the sum total of its appeal. 

Technically, Rense favors well-lit shots that let readers see the details of a room; she rejects views from behind sofas, which shut the reader out. If she says, "This would look good at night," that's a command to do one of AD's trademark twilight or "blue light" pictures, snapped in the 10 minutes between dusk and nightfall. Except for celebrities, Rense has always disliked seeing residents in interiors, believing they spoiled the fantasy: "It couldn't be yours if it was theirs," she says. But now that other magazines show people more, she does too.

What Rense won't do is send editors to style the pictures with carloads of accessories, a standard industry practice. At AD, the designer or photographer does the styling; no editor is present at the shoot. (And, no, AD does not send the same cymbidium orchid from place to place.) Originally, AD couldn't afford stylists -- it didn't even pay for pictures until 1977. Today, Rense says, "I believe in the singular vision."

Designers whose work has not made it into Digest blame Rense's loyalty to a rat pack of designer pals, people who, former employees say, have bought her affection with lavish gifts, even diamonds and a sable. "It is true I was sent a fur coat," Rense says carefully. "It was from a decorator I've known a long time. It wasn't sable -- it was mink. I gave it to charity." As for the diamond earrings, they were from a man "I was once engaged to," she says. "Definitely not a decorator." She does accept gifts, she says, from decorators who are personal friends. And in exchange: "I send decorators very expensive gifts. It never occurs to designers that they're rejected because they're not good enough. Anyone who knows me knows you can give me 20 fur coats, diamonds -- it won't get you in the magazine." 

Certainly, no one needs pull to have work considered. Rense sees every single submission. "We try to be fair," she sighs. "Some deserve no comment, they're so bad." Only once in two sessions does she bestow an obvious favor: "It's not this designer's best work. Can we save it by reshooting?" A few sensitive decisions are postponed. But for the most part she bites the bullet. "Let's save him from himself," she says, turning down one regular. A submission from a stranger gets equal time, but a star is not born. "Can't, can't, can't," she says despairingly. 

Now she's getting testy. One rejection after another. "Is our inventory that low?" "He believes less is more, sorry!" "N.F.A.D." (meaning "Not for Architectural Digest"). Cliches (bleached floors, white-canvas upholstery, chopped pillows and ficus trees in one room) disqualify several submissions. A shoot by the photographer Derry Moore, Rense's invaluable scout in England, pleases her, only . . . something is missing. "Is Derry resisting us on the bedroom?" she asks. As AD readers know, Rense wants to see the bedroom. "You must imagine you could entertain, have dinner, and go to bed," one of her photographers says.

Rense gives thumbs up to a grand garden, telling her art director to crop out the undistinguished garden ornaments. She also O.K.'s the home of a major American family -- "but only the exterior." Finally something really pleases her. It's a coup -- the restored cabin of an important historical figure. "Great!" she says, banging the light box with her palms. "I want it all."

With a little luck, the designers selected will see their work run in 12 months. "The inventory is the high-wire act," Rense says. "You need enough for an interesting orchestration. But if you have too much on hand, people get mad." If a designer is ill with AIDS, she does her best to run his work as soon as possible. If he dies, the work will not be shown, because, she says, with peculiar logic, "then it's not a service to the reader."

One house she has every intention of running is her own, situated close to the Pacific in Santa Barbara, a 75-mile commute she makes with a car and driver provided by Cleon T. (Bud) Knapp, chairman of Knapp Communications. Curiosity about Rense's personal taste is intense. Her last house, in Beverly Hills, appeared as a cover story in AD 10 years ago. It was a nouveau-California tour de force, choreographed by her good friend Sally Sirkin Lewis, with faux stone and shiny glass, overstuffed sofas, Oriental tchotchkes and lots of pillows. The Lewis look has been so influential that AD still receives an avalanche of photos from imitators. But Rense insists that the decor was "for the editor of Architectural Digest -- it wasn't me."

The Santa Barbara house -- which she did herself with a little advice from four designers -- features the folk art and primitive furniture she's been buying for a decade, and used to sell in the mid-80's when she briefly owned Country Manor Antiques in Montecito, near Santa Barbara (an ill-conceived venture that took her deep into conflict-of-interest territory). The throw pillows have been replaced by old quilts and hooked rugs. The only things that shine are a few pieces of old mercury glass.

Oddly, despite the current popularity of "country" magazines, Rense didn't think her readers were ready for tree bark and knotholes until 1988, when she gave it a big play in her annual country-house issue. Now that 

le tout 

Hollywood, from Candice Bergen to Richard Dreyfuss, is busy gathering twigs -- so will AD more frequently.

Not that readers look to AD for trends (Rense hates both the word and the idea). Marie Daniel, a Sioux Falls, S.D., subscriber who collects inexpensive Depression glass, says: "I enjoy reading about things I could never afford. It's fun to see how the other half lives." Mrs. Charles Williams, a Paducah, Ky., subscriber and proud owner of traditional-style Baker furniture, says: "The magazine makes me feel my taste is better. When I visit houses I can tell what's right and what's wrong." She also gets a kick out of looking at the editor in chief's photo every month. "Paige what's-her-name is so good-looking. I always want to see what her hairdo is. She does a lot with herself."

INDEED. UNTIL NOW, THE editor in chief of Architectural Digest has never told the real story about her early life. "Paige started out deep in the hole," says her husband, Arthur Rense. "She survived by blocking out things that made her unhappy." She was born in an Iowa farm town on May 4, 1929. When she was about a year old, her mother, a woman of Danish descent, who sometimes used the last name of Jensen, gave up her baby (who was named Jean or Louise or Violet, no one can remember) for adoption to a Des Moines couple Rense deems "an unfortunate choice." She has vowed never to utter their name. They called her Patricia. 

"They were poor, that was all right," Rense says. "My adoptive mother was a functioning retarded person. She did her best. My adoptive father made our lives a living hell. They're both dead now." If they had any aspirations for her, Rense says, "they were for me to marry, perhaps, the manager of a bowling alley, have a little house, and three or four children."

When Patricia was 12 or 13 the family moved to Los Angeles. In junior high, a surprised teacher told her she had the highest I.Q. in the class. At 15, finding her home life intolerable, she dropped out of Hollywood High and set up on her own in a furnished room, lying about her age to get work ("I was an usherette at every theater on Hollywood Boulevard"). She called herself Paige because it had a nice ring to it, and adopted different last names depending on what movie she had just seen. Sometimes she used Jensen: when Paige was around 19, she finally met her real mother, who was dying.

In her late teens she was married briefly -- the man's name doesn't come to mind. In the early 1950's a friend, an Army wife, alerted her to a typing job at an American radio station in Tokyo. She took a boat there and returned to New York a year later with David Thomas, a soldier, to whom she was wed briefly. Paige, who never went beyond her freshman year in high school, began claiming to have a B.A. in English from Cal State. "I had to invent a background to better myself," she says, coming clean. "At least I never pretended it was Vassar."

In 1955, she "blundered" into a low-level editorial job at Water World, a short-lived skin-diving magazine. There, the managing editor, Arthur Rense, ran her first story. They were married two years later. 

"Arthur was my university," says Rense, who soon went on to write a paperback, "Hollywood Secrets to Beauty and Fashion," and put in stints as an editor at a teen-agers' magazine called Dig; as publicity director of Cole of California (swimsuits); and as advertising director of Viviane Woodard, a direct-sales cosmetics company. In the late 60's she decided to stay home in suburban Thousand Oaks, attending to her husband and his three sons by a previous marriage. "I was determined to bake bread," she says. It was as close as she would get to the M-G-M family of her dreams.

Rense calls her domestic phase "the worst two years of my life." Soon she was hitting the typewriter, turning out a novel she'd rather forget and two articles for Cosmopolitan. One was a single girl's guide to manners called "Is That the Right Fork?" The other, "Ciao, Sherry!," retains a certain interest. A short story, it told the tale of a naive, virgin copywriter and her emeralds-are-a-girl's-best-friend nymphomaniac roommate -- two characters who, like Rense, were desperate to amount to something. 

"Ciao, Sherry!," with its references to Women's Wear Daily and the international rich, demonstrated Rense's fascination with the emerging jet set, an interest that would help her get her next job and keep it. In 1970, she heard that Architectural Digest needed a writer. Paige Rense, who has probably delivered this zinger many times, pauses for effect: "I said, 'I never heard of it.' "

Not many people had. founded in 1920, The Architectural Digest was a trade magazine spawned by the California building boom (the "The" was dropped in 1967). With pictures supplied gratis by advertisers, a spanking-new soda fountain was as likely to be featured as a grand Spanish-style mansion. In 1965 it was sold to the founder's grandson, Bud Knapp, then 27, who had worked for the magazine on and off since he was a teen-ager. The price was $65,000.

Convinced that a new class of wealthy cultural consumers had replaced yesterday's nobility, Knapp wanted Digest to compete with European art publications -- and said so in wordy editorials. The magazine added the subtitle: The Home as a Work of Art, but in the fall of 1970, when Rense was interviewed for the job of associate editor, the houses shown in it still were handouts or also-rans from other publications.

Knapp's first meeting with Rense has assumed mythical status. Rense remembers Knapp asking her opinion of the magazine. "I told him tactfully," she says, rolling her eyes and sighing deeply, "that the magazine was amateurish and not interesting, that it was time for decorators to be stars." Knapp was impressed. "She wasn't the naive little girl she pretends to be," he laughs. "I know that act by now. She was a very smart journalist and publicist. She knew commerce and media. She was not hired because she was a writer or knew interior design or architecture. She had people qualities." 

Rense started work in October 1970 -- bringing the editorial staff to a grand total of four. Even for her, there is culture shock on revisiting the pages of those early issues, with their fur rugs and blankets, hairy throw pillows, and elephant table bases. "Oh, Lord," she says. "You couldn't stop the zebras."

Events quickly took a strange turn. A little after midnight on April 9, 1971, Architectural Digest's 37-year-old editor, James Bradley Little, was shot dead in his auto outside of Club John, on North La Cienega Boulevard. Two men had climbed into the back seat, robbed Little and his companion, the playwright Gant Gaither, of money and jewelry. As they fled, Little was shot in the back of the head. (This bizarre incident has found its way into Rense's latest book, a mystery novel with the working title "To Die For," in which the victim is the editor of a decorating magazine.)

Appointed editor by Knapp, Rense wasted no time making changes. She ended the practice of trading coverage for ads, and more dramatic covers trumpeted a new era. With great finesse, Rense phased out Bud Knapp's editorials. "They didn't contribute anything to the magazine or to his reputation," she says, "so I just put a rejection slip on his copy one month, and that was that."

Pictures were Rense's first priority -- and still are (to this day, she is the only AD editor who visits houses under consideration). But to get "virgin" houses, never-before published, Rense had to break the stranglehold on top designers that Conde Nast's House & Garden had. She made a two-pronged attack on San Francisco (piloted by the power designer Anthony Hail) and New York (where the late designer Angelo Donghia opened solid-core doors for her). Designers were susceptible to her advances, miffed that their work was being stockpiled in what the decorator John Saladino calls "the Conde Nast abyss." "You couldn't complain," says the designer Jay Spectre. "It was like the old A.T.&T.; -- the only game in town." 

Spectre was one of the first to defect, followed by a group of designers now known as Rense's New York coterie, which also includes Michael de Santis, Robert Metzger, Melvin Dwork and the firm of Bray-Schaible. In return for an exclusive on Spectre's East Hampton house, Rense promised him a cover. Instead of fracturing pictures graphically, as House & Garden did, she published houses in album form, moving from entrance hall (never "entry") to living room, library (never "den"), dining room and bedroom. She further seduced photographers and designers with prominent credit lines. Deferential interviews with designers made them stars -- as promised.

With no mentors to guide her, except the eclectic mix of decorators most eager to be featured in her magazine, Rense learned as she went along, often feigning expertise. She watched her decorators at work, and took them along when she visited antiques shops and museums. Gradually, she educated her own taste, which her critics say reflects the gaudier side of some of the designers she cultivated. But that touch of vulgarity may have a great deal to do with the magazine's success.

When it came to deciding what readers wanted, Rense needed no help. Assuming that they would be as interested as she was in how movie stars lived, for example, she served up celebrity visits with the likes of John Wayne, Joan Crawford, Woody Allen, Burt Lancaster and Kirk Douglas. (Try as she might, she never got Bette Davis.) "It was voyeurism in spades," says a Rense-watcher. And it worked. 

Circulation and ads rose, along with recognition. But the camaraderie Rense established with her small staff deteriorated as she became a public persona, doing the social minuet, signing up influential socialites as "contributing editors," appearing on TV talk shows. Meanwhile, she went through a painful divorce from Arthur Rense (whom she remarried in 1987). Soon, several former staffers agree, she became distant. There was "an atmosphere of fear," even "terror." Moody and mercurial, she was deemed "tyrannical." New employees were told by colleagues that it wasn't a good idea to keep children's photos on one's desk, because Rense didn't have children; that if she was going to a press party, no one else should; that you shouldn't get in the elevator if she was on it. Dismissing it all, Rense says, "We all have problems with authority figures."

The firings at AD became legendary. A prophetic passage in "Ciao, Sherry!" described a tough office manager "who severed heads quickly, cleanly, without last rites. She just pulled the black hood over her head and chopped." The lines could have been written about AD, from reports of former employees who claim they were axed without warning by personnel, then given a few hours to clear their desks and leave the building. Rense insists that the quick boot was company policy.

No one, however, could argue that the magazine wasn't thriving -- and Rense was the reason. Although many people have toiled for her behind the scenes, doing virtually all the editing and ghost-writing her editor's letter, drafting the copy for her 12 AD books and even, on occasion, autographing them for her, just about everything was her vision, her concept. By 1979, advertising revenues had hit $10.3 million. With 1,158 ad pages that year, AD was getting dangerously close to House & Garden's 1,417. (Ten years later, with 1,889 pages, it had left HG, with its 990 pages, far behind.) 

Reportedly, Rense rejected overtures from Conde Nast and Hearst, preferring to stay at Knapp, where she enjoyed autonomy -- and protected it zealously. Knapp, who calls Rense "domineering," felt her wrath once after bringing in a management consultant: "If I have to answer to him," she stormed, "I'll go across the street and work for Prudential." 

Moonlighting for Knapp, she gave her all to his 1975 acquisition, Bon Appetit, whose masthead still lists her as "founding editor." Although she was opposed to his 1981 acquisition of the American edition of Geo, the glossy German travel-art magazine, she gave it her best shot -- to no avail. The magazine folded in 1985. But Rense was already running out of steam. "I was tired," she says. "I began asking my business manager, 'When can I get out?' "

Rense snapped out of her lethargy in 1983, when Conde Nast rolled out a redesigned House & Garden. Going after AD's upscale audience, the magazine cut its circulation to 660,000 and adopted the portfolio-of-homes approach used by AD. To Rense's fury, the remake won an award from the American Society of Magazine Editors, the industry's highest honor. 

"They were arrogant to steal my format," she says. "It made me mad." Rense counterattacked. In June 1985, AD published a special issue devoted entirely to the English country house. It was a smashing success, and Rense began putting out an annual country house issue. Next came the annual New York issue (November) and an international issue (January). To counter AD's image as nothing more than a picture book, the magazine paid top dollar to recruit writers like John Updike, Margaret Atwood and William Styron. 

Rense was on a roll. Conde Nast, meanwhile, struggled. In 1986, House & Garden's editor, Louis Oliver Gropp, was out. Anna Wintour was brought in from British Vogue to pinch-hit. She swiftly changed the magazine's name to HG and developed an idiosyncratic blend of fashion and interior design. Though probably the wave of the future, it was too much of a mishmash for the stodgy china and crystal advertiser crowd. AD had won both rounds.

Rense kept up the offensive, though. In quick succession she put out a trial spinoff called AD Travels. When it failed as a stand-alone, she stuffed it into the magazine, where advertisers had wanted it all along. Then she introduced regular architecture sections, and in December will bring out an all-architecture theme issue. In April, her Academy Awards Collectors Issue, showing the homes of such Golden Age stars as Charles Chaplin, Mary Pickford, Gloria Swanson, and Gary Cooper, turned out to be the magazine's second-largest newsstand seller ever -- surpassed only by the December 1981 cover of the Reagans' private quarters in the White House.

While the competition obsesses about beating AD at the newsstand, Rense now spends much of her time dreaming up promotional projects to generate miscellaneous revenue. With the magazine industry in recession, AD's advertising will decline slightly in November for the first time in years, and the brains at AD are working overtime to keep their weighty ship on an even keel. In the process, the magazine sometimes appears to obliterate the sacrosanct divide between the business and editorial sides of the enterprise. The traditional magazine "separation of church and state can't work," Bud Knapp explains. "Editors have to be more responsive to marketing."

The responsive Rense came up with the AD 100, a decorators' source guide inspired by the Forbes 400 (or, some critics say, by a decorators' source guide shopped to Knapp Communications by John C. Aves, a Chicago ad man and fishing buddy of Bud Knapp's). Presented to readers as a kind of 13th issue, the AD 100 ruffled feathers by leaving out chintz royals like the New York firm of Parish-Hadley, but it was a major success: its 133 pages of ads will keep AD's 1990 ad figures from falling below last year's. Next year's bonus will be a guide to the top 100 architects, a Machiavellian move that will enlist the support of Rense's most supercilious critics.

Rense's latest brainstorm, and potentially most controversial idea, is the AD Collection, to be unveiled in the December issue. It's a haute mail-order catalogue featuring 26 antiques and works of art priced from $15,000 to $800,000, most of them from AD advertisers. In a kind of twist on the logo-stamped novelties that magazines often peddle in their pages, AD will offer readers not mugs, aprons or calendars, but a pair of rare Adam mirrors, a 17th-century Japanese screen or a Sheridan-style breakfront with palm-frond top.

"Why not give dealers a whole new clientele, and open a world for the reader who may not have a decorator?" Rense rationalizes.  "They can feel confident about what they buy." The dealers pay nothing for the honor of inclusion -- it's not considered advertising. If an item sells, however, the 20 percent commission that would normally go to a decorator (so far, the decorators are simmering in silence) will be split between charity (5 percent) and the magazine (15 percent) -- opening up a whole new source of revenue. "We'll make a nice profit," says Rense, sounding just like the member of the Knapp board she is. (She is also exploring the idea of having AD sell grand house plans, by master architects of the past and present.)

"Leave it to Paige to push the envelope," says an astonished John Mack Carter, president of the American Society of Magazine Editors and editor in chief of Good Housekeeping. As for the ethics involved, he says, "It's not a conflict so long as it is conducted as a service to the reader and not a profit center." Carter pauses. "Paige Rense, merchant -- interesting idea."

That may not be the only surprising change that AD readers see in the 90's. With the lines drawn in the sands of Malibu, the Italian Riviera and the Hamptons, the next decade will be as interesting for how design magazines deal with the new coolness toward conspicuous consumption as for how they compete for houses to publish and for market share.

Many people wonder, as does Nancy Novogrod, editor in chief of the newly resurgent HG, whether "the house as a work of art, perfectly composed, pristine and untouched, isn't old hat now." Paige Rense, den mother to the "$200,000 doesn't go very far" decorator, knows the stuffing is coming out of the excessively rich look -- Knapp's own consumer studies have told her so. So AD will look different -- and in time, so will the taste of its readers. "Paige Rense can't dictate how designers design," Bud Knapp says, "but she influences by what she chooses."

Insiders ask, however, whether Rense's loyalty to designers who stuck with her during the House & Garden wars isn't standing in the way of a fresh look, whether AD wouldn't be better positioned for the 90's with an editor who has fewer political debts. Bud Knapp insists he is in no rush for her to take off her spurs. "I want her to keep working as long as she can type."

When the woman Knapp calls "the keeper of the sacred flame" does go, it won't be with a pile of company stock: other than her employee profit sharing plan, she has no equity in the company that has given her boss a net worth of $200 million. This is a sore subject. "Once, Bud told me all his friends want to know why I get all the publicity," Rense says. "I told him, all my friends want to know why he gets all the money."

But Rense is not talking retirement. Nor does she see AD as king of the hill, invulnerable to attack. In her office, she flounces her blue denim cowgirl skirt, leans forward squarely, and digs her boot heels in the beige wall-to-wall. "I'm still David, not Goliath. Conde Nast and Hearst have billions trained at me. I am outmanned and outmonied." But is she worried? "Oh God, no!" she exclaims, those eyes widening. "They're never going to beat me!"
snippet:
Miss Page Rense
Architectural Digest
Los Angeles, Calif.
Dear Miss Rense:

Although I could never afford the lifestyle of the people who live in the sumptuous homes you show, I am an avid fan of your fabulous magazine. I especially like to see how celebrities live and wonder which issue I should buy to get a look at Candy and Aaron Spelling's quintessential new Hollywood home, built with profits from "Dynasty" and "Love Boat." I read in a gossip column that their mansion is bigger than the White House, cost over $50 million and has its own bowling alley. 

Hoping to hear from you soon.
 A Decorating Fan.
Dear Fan,

Your letter is deeply appreciated, since every genuine letter to the editor we receive means my hard-working staff has one less to create for our Letters column.

It is gratifying to learn that you enjoy our celebrity features, since, believe me, it is not easy finding well-known people whose taste lives up to our standards.

There is a common misconception that Architectural Digest glorifies conspicuous consumption, which couldn't be farther from the truth. In my two decades here, we have occasionally published some grand houses, but our motto for the 90's is, Bigger Isn't Better, except in circulation, advertising and miscellaneous revenues.

Regarding the Spelling house, at present we have no plans to publish it -- which has nothing to do with my disdain for bowling.

As a consolation, I am enclosing some tips from a book I'm thinking of writing next weekend (it will be my 15th, if my assistant has counted correctly) . It will be called "You Don't Say: Paige Rense's Guide to Taboo Celebrity House Talk."

 -- Don't say "home," say "house."

-- Don't use trite words like "lifestyle," "sumptuous," "fabulous" or "quintessential."

 -- Always spell Paige with an i.

 Cordially,
 Paige Rense, editor in chief

It's easy to parody Paige Rense -- to make fun of her legendary no-nos, her concocted reader letters, her magazine's pretentious tone and extravagant taste, and the idea of one person's passing judgment on thousands of houses every year -- particularly a woman who didn't know Gaudi from gaudy when she started. But you can't underestimate her accomplishments. In 19 years at the helm of Architectural Digest, with meager magazine experience and an initial operating budget that wasn't much larger than one competitor's annual taxi allotment, Rense has turned a marginal building-trades magazine published by Knapp Communications into a top-of-the-line voyeur's bible -- the National Geographic of interior design, art and antiques. Between 1971 and 1989, she has taken circulation from 50,000 to 625,000, and advertising revenues from less than $1 million to $46 million. And all this in a magazine backwater called Los Angeles.

Today Architectural Digest stands supreme among the "shelter magazines" -- the thick and glossy periodicals devoted to decorating and home furnishings, a multibillion-dollar industry in the United States. Rense earns a salary estimated at about $600,000 -- a queen's ransom in the magazine world. Exposure in AD has become so important to decorators that she has seen some completed jobs before the client has. Decorators the world over take a rejection of their work by Rense as the ultimate snub ("a maniac" one of them called her after finding himself left out of "The AD 100," the magazine's recent issue devoted to the top 100 designers whose work has appeared in its pages). Yet none dare cross her, for fear of winding up in Rolodex limbo. ("Strike him off all of our lists now!" she has ruled.) 

The magazine casts a mesmerizing spell over its readers. It isn't hip like Metropolitan Home (circulation 701,000), with its witty mix of basic-Biedermeier and Mies-to-go; it isn't "how-to" like House Beautiful (circulation, 932,000); it wouldn't be caught dead showing $500,000 his-and-her kitchens or trendy lofts like the young-but-rich HG (circulation, 619,900), and it has none of the torn curtains or socks under the bed in the throwaway-chic World of Interiors (circulation, 73,000).

No, Architectural Digest -- "The International Magazine of Fine Interior Design" -- is one continuous house tour, where glitz and refinement cohabit happily. Cher's house -- or houses (AD has printed four of them so far) -- is just as welcome as Baron Thyssen-Bornemisza's private museum and Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother's house at Sandringham (coming in AD in January).

The magazine really came into its own in the early 1980's, when more-is-more began to replace less-is-more as a (pardon the word) lifestyle credo. "Money was suddenly beautiful, and the Digest was the only upscale design magazine," observes Steven Cohn of Media Industry Newsletter.

It wasn't long before less pricey shelter magazines moved into the same "affluential" (a Rense coinage) neighborhood, but Digest has remained in a class by itself.

"Pretentious" is the word some use to describe Rense's drawing-room-drama approach, especially her appetite for opulence in present-day interior decoration. "It's like a Potemkin village," says Ira Levy, senior vice-president for creative corporate development at Estee Lauder. "Everything is too perfect."

But love the magazine -- or love to dish it -- AD is a must read. "It's glued to everyone's coffee table," says Mario Buatta, the decorator, who has had his share of glory in it. "My clients treasure it," says Patricia Crane, a Bryn Mawr, Pa., designer whose work has never appeared in Digest. "This is success," she adds with a sniff, "what they aspire to." 

 "Aspire" doesn't begin to cover it. According to one story, which may even be true, a Beverly Hills woman on her deathbed received a call from her daughter, who said she'd be delayed coming over because Architectural Digest was photographing her house. In that case, said the mother. "Don't worry about me. Take your time." 

THE SIGN ON THE wooden door that leads into Architectural Digest's viewing room warns away unauthorized personnel with a stern "Do Not Enter." They don't. Here, 30 floors above Wilshire Boulevard, is the heart of the AD dream machine. File cabinets filled with photos line the walls and divide the room; along one wall runs a deep shelf holding a row of light boxes. Three to four times a month, the fate of thousands of designers, photographers and houses is decided. There is no jury, just the judge -- Paige Rense, who has seen it all.

At the appointed hour Rense sweeps in with a "Hi, darlin' " for her art director, Thomas Sullivan. The greeting reflects the "New West" Rense: she just bought land in Jackson Hole, Wyo., and she's negotiating to buy a house in Santa Fe, N.M., and these days she favors denim cowgirl skirts, boots and a slow drawl.

Her looks are deceiving. Some days she seems as plain as a movie star before breakfast; large glasses disguise a hint of sadness in her eyes. But then suddenly, for an audience, for a camera, for a decorator passing through "on his way to Pittsburgh," she lights up -- and 

heeeeeeere's 

Paige: extremely photogenic, she has large blue eyes that never blink at a strobe flash, a pug nose, a vivacious Ginger Rogers smile, and a souffle of blond frosted hair.

Like women of her generation who found it smart to play dumb (Rense admits to 57 but is actually 61), she often lapses into a cute little-girl's voice. She talks softly and lets deputies carry the big stick. Constantly called on to judge the creative efforts of others, she has developed a reassuring ooh-and-aah delivery of "Oh, how wonderful," "Oh, how marvelous." When she really likes something, though, she'll bang both hands on the nearest surface, palms down, and exclaim, "Great!"

Right now, the pictures are laid out on the light boxes for Rense's review. Her back slightly curved from years of hunching over these viewing boxes, she works her way quickly from left to right, as her art director, "photographer liaison" (AD has no photo editor) and assistants stand by quietly noting her decisions. Then she starts over, moving rightward, until the current backlog is disposed of -- one way or another. The little-girl voice is never used here. And her decision is final. The absence of give and take is awesome. 

The staff can't predict what she'll like. Using her legendary intuition, she calculates at a glance the uniqueness of the design, the impact of the photographs, the prominence of the resident, the importance of the designer -- and whir, whir, click, click -- the sum total of its appeal. 

Technically, Rense favors well-lit shots that let readers see the details of a room; she rejects views from behind sofas, which shut the reader out. If she says, "This would look good at night," that's a command to do one of AD's trademark twilight or "blue light" pictures, snapped in the 10 minutes between dusk and nightfall. Except for celebrities, Rense has always disliked seeing residents in interiors, believing they spoiled the fantasy: "It couldn't be yours if it was theirs," she says. But now that other magazines show people more, she does too.

What Rense won't do is send editors to style the pictures with carloads of accessories, a standard industry practice. At AD, the designer or photographer does the styling; no editor is present at the shoot. (And, no, AD does not send the same cymbidium orchid from place to place.) Originally, AD couldn't afford stylists -- it didn't even pay for pictures until 1977. Today, Rense says, "I believe in the singular vision."

Designers whose work has not made it into Digest blame Rense's loyalty to a rat pack of designer pals, people who, former employees say, have bought her affection with lavish gifts, even diamonds and a sable. "It is true I was sent a fur coat," Rense says carefully. "It was from a decorator I've known a long time. It wasn't sable -- it was mink. I gave it to charity." As for the diamond earrings, they were from a man "I was once engaged to," she says. "Definitely not a decorator." She does accept gifts, she says, from decorators who are personal friends. And in exchange: "I send decorators very expensive gifts. It never occurs to designers that they're rejected because they're not good enough. Anyone who knows me knows you can give me 20 fur coats, diamonds -- it won't get you in the magazine." 

Certainly, no one needs pull to have work considered. Rense sees every single submission. "We try to be fair," she sighs. "Some deserve no comment, they're so bad." Only once in two sessions does she bestow an obvious favor: "It's not this designer's best work. Can we save it by reshooting?" A few sensitive decisions are postponed. But for the most part she bites the bullet. "Let's save him from himself," she says, turning down one regular. A submission from a stranger gets equal time, but a star is not born. "Can't, can't, can't," she says despairingly. 

Now she's getting testy. One rejection after another. "Is our inventory that low?" "He believes less is more, sorry!" "N.F.A.D." (meaning "Not for Architectural Digest"). Cliches (bleached floors, white-canvas upholstery, chopped pillows and ficus trees in one room) disqualify several submissions. A shoot by the photographer Derry Moore, Rense's invaluable scout in England, pleases her, only . . . something is missing. "Is Derry resisting us on the bedroom?" she asks. As AD readers know, Rense wants to see the bedroom. "You must imagine you could entertain, have dinner, and go to bed," one of her photographers says.

Rense gives thumbs up to a grand garden, telling her art director to crop out the undistinguished garden ornaments. She also O.K.'s the home of a major American family -- "but only the exterior." Finally something really pleases her. It's a coup -- the restored cabin of an important historical figure. "Great!" she says, banging the light box with her palms. "I want it all."

With a little luck, the designers selected will see their work run in 12 months. "The inventory is the high-wire act," Rense says. "You need enough for an interesting orchestration. But if you have too much on hand, people get mad." If a designer is ill with AIDS, she does her best to run his work as soon as possible. If he dies, the work will not be shown, because, she says, with peculiar logic, "then it's not a service to the reader."

One house she has every intention of running is her own, situated close to the Pacific in Santa Barbara, a 75-mile commute she makes with a car and driver provided by Cleon T. (Bud) Knapp, chairman of Knapp Communications. Curiosity about Rense's personal taste is intense. Her last house, in Beverly Hills, appeared as a cover story in AD 10 years ago. It was a nouveau-California tour de force, choreographed by her good friend Sally Sirkin Lewis, with faux stone and shiny glass, overstuffed sofas, Oriental tchotchkes and lots of pillows. The Lewis look has been so influential that AD still receives an avalanche of photos from imitators. But Rense insists that the decor was "for the editor of Architectural Digest -- it wasn't me."

The Santa Barbara house -- which she did herself with a little advice from four designers -- features the folk art and primitive furniture she's been buying for a decade, and used to sell in the mid-80's when she briefly owned Country Manor Antiques in Montecito, near Santa Barbara (an ill-conceived venture that took her deep into conflict-of-interest territory). The throw pillows have been replaced by old quilts and hooked rugs. The only things that shine are a few pieces of old mercury glass.

Oddly, despite the current popularity of "country" magazines, Rense didn't think her readers were ready for tree bark and knotholes until 1988, when she gave it a big play in her annual country-house issue. Now that 

le tout 

Hollywood, from Candice Bergen to Richard Dreyfuss, is busy gathering twigs -- so will AD more frequently.

Not that readers look to AD for trends (Rense hates both the word and the idea). Marie Daniel, a Sioux Falls, S.D., subscriber who collects inexpensive Depression glass, says: "I enjoy reading about things I could never afford. It's fun to see how the other half lives." Mrs. Charles Williams, a Paducah, Ky., subscriber and proud owner of traditional-style Baker furniture, says: "The magazine makes me feel my taste is better. When I visit houses I can tell what's right and what's wrong." She also gets a kick out of looking at the editor in chief's photo every month. "Paige what's-her-name is so good-looking. I always want to see what her hairdo is. She does a lot with herself."

INDEED. UNTIL NOW, THE editor in chief of Architectural Digest has never told the real story about her early life. "Paige started out deep in the hole," says her husband, Arthur Rense. "She survived by blocking out things that made her unhappy." She was born in an Iowa farm town on May 4, 1929. When she was about a year old, her mother, a woman of Danish descent, who sometimes used the last name of Jensen, gave up her baby (who was named Jean or Louise or Violet, no one can remember) for adoption to a Des Moines couple Rense deems "an unfortunate choice." She has vowed never to utter their name. They called her Patricia. 

"They were poor, that was all right," Rense says. "My adoptive mother was a functioning retarded person. She did her best. My adoptive father made our lives a living hell. They're both dead now." If they had any aspirations for her, Rense says, "they were for me to marry, perhaps, the manager of a bowling alley, have a little house, and three or four children."

When Patricia was 12 or 13 the family moved to Los Angeles. In junior high, a surprised teacher told her she had the highest I.Q. in the class. At 15, finding her home life intolerable, she dropped out of Hollywood High and set up on her own in a furnished room, lying about her age to get work ("I was an usherette at every theater on Hollywood Boulevard"). She called herself Paige because it had a nice ring to it, and adopted different last names depending on what movie she had just seen. Sometimes she used Jensen: when Paige was around 19, she finally met her real mother, who was dying.

In her late teens she was married briefly -- the man's name doesn't come to mind. In the early 1950's a friend, an Army wife, alerted her to a typing job at an American radio station in Tokyo. She took a boat there and returned to New York a year later with David Thomas, a soldier, to whom she was wed briefly. Paige, who never went beyond her freshman year in high school, began claiming to have a B.A. in English from Cal State. "I had to invent a background to better myself," she says, coming clean. "At least I never pretended it was Vassar."

In 1955, she "blundered" into a low-level editorial job at Water World, a short-lived skin-diving magazine. There, the managing editor, Arthur Rense, ran her first story. They were married two years later. 

"Arthur was my university," says Rense, who soon went on to write a paperback, "Hollywood Secrets to Beauty and Fashion," and put in stints as an editor at a teen-agers' magazine called Dig; as publicity director of Cole of California (swimsuits); and as advertising director of Viviane Woodard, a direct-sales cosmetics company. In the late 60's she decided to stay home in suburban Thousand Oaks, attending to her husband and his three sons by a previous marriage. "I was determined to bake bread," she says. It was as close as she would get to the M-G-M family of her dreams.

Rense calls her domestic phase "the worst two years of my life." Soon she was hitting the typewriter, turning out a novel she'd rather forget and two articles for Cosmopolitan. One was a single girl's guide to manners called "Is That the Right Fork?" The other, "Ciao, Sherry!," retains a certain interest. A short story, it told the tale of a naive, virgin copywriter and her emeralds-are-a-girl's-best-friend nymphomaniac roommate -- two characters who, like Rense, were desperate to amount to something. 

"Ciao, Sherry!," with its references to Women's Wear Daily and the international rich, demonstrated Rense's fascination with the emerging jet set, an interest that would help her get her next job and keep it. In 1970, she heard that Architectural Digest needed a writer. Paige Rense, who has probably delivered this zinger many times, pauses for effect: "I said, 'I never heard of it.' "

Not many people had. founded in 1920, The Architectural Digest was a trade magazine spawned by the California building boom (the "The" was dropped in 1967). With pictures supplied gratis by advertisers, a spanking-new soda fountain was as likely to be featured as a grand Spanish-style mansion. In 1965 it was sold to the founder's grandson, Bud Knapp, then 27, who had worked for the magazine on and off since he was a teen-ager. The price was $65,000.

Convinced that a new class of wealthy cultural consumers had replaced yesterday's nobility, Knapp wanted Digest to compete with European art publications -- and said so in wordy editorials. The magazine added the subtitle: The Home as a Work of Art, but in the fall of 1970, when Rense was interviewed for the job of associate editor, the houses shown in it still were handouts or also-rans from other publications.

Knapp's first meeting with Rense has assumed mythical status. Rense remembers Knapp asking her opinion of the magazine. "I told him tactfully," she says, rolling her eyes and sighing deeply, "that the magazine was amateurish and not interesting, that it was time for decorators to be stars." Knapp was impressed. "She wasn't the naive little girl she pretends to be," he laughs. "I know that act by now. She was a very smart journalist and publicist. She knew commerce and media. She was not hired because she was a writer or knew interior design or architecture. She had people qualities." 

Rense started work in October 1970 -- bringing the editorial staff to a grand total of four. Even for her, there is culture shock on revisiting the pages of those early issues, with their fur rugs and blankets, hairy throw pillows, and elephant table bases. "Oh, Lord," she says. "You couldn't stop the zebras."

Events quickly took a strange turn. A little after midnight on April 9, 1971, Architectural Digest's 37-year-old editor, James Bradley Little, was shot dead in his auto outside of Club John, on North La Cienega Boulevard. Two men had climbed into the back seat, robbed Little and his companion, the playwright Gant Gaither, of money and jewelry. As they fled, Little was shot in the back of the head. (This bizarre incident has found its way into Rense's latest book, a mystery novel with the working title "To Die For," in which the victim is the editor of a decorating magazine.)

Appointed editor by Knapp, Rense wasted no time making changes. She ended the practice of trading coverage for ads, and more dramatic covers trumpeted a new era. With great finesse, Rense phased out Bud Knapp's editorials. "They didn't contribute anything to the magazine or to his reputation," she says, "so I just put a rejection slip on his copy one month, and that was that."

Pictures were Rense's first priority -- and still are (to this day, she is the only AD editor who visits houses under consideration). But to get "virgin" houses, never-before published, Rense had to break the stranglehold on top designers that Conde Nast's House & Garden had. She made a two-pronged attack on San Francisco (piloted by the power designer Anthony Hail) and New York (where the late designer Angelo Donghia opened solid-core doors for her). Designers were susceptible to her advances, miffed that their work was being stockpiled in what the decorator John Saladino calls "the Conde Nast abyss." "You couldn't complain," says the designer Jay Spectre. "It was like the old A.T.&T.; -- the only game in town." 

Spectre was one of the first to defect, followed by a group of designers now known as Rense's New York coterie, which also includes Michael de Santis, Robert Metzger, Melvin Dwork and the firm of Bray-Schaible. In return for an exclusive on Spectre's East Hampton house, Rense promised him a cover. Instead of fracturing pictures graphically, as House & Garden did, she published houses in album form, moving from entrance hall (never "entry") to living room, library (never "den"), dining room and bedroom. She further seduced photographers and designers with prominent credit lines. Deferential interviews with designers made them stars -- as promised.

With no mentors to guide her, except the eclectic mix of decorators most eager to be featured in her magazine, Rense learned as she went along, often feigning expertise. She watched her decorators at work, and took them along when she visited antiques shops and museums. Gradually, she educated her own taste, which her critics say reflects the gaudier side of some of the designers she cultivated. But that touch of vulgarity may have a great deal to do with the magazine's success.

When it came to deciding what readers wanted, Rense needed no help. Assuming that they would be as interested as she was in how movie stars lived, for example, she served up celebrity visits with the likes of John Wayne, Joan Crawford, Woody Allen, Burt Lancaster and Kirk Douglas. (Try as she might, she never got Bette Davis.) "It was voyeurism in spades," says a Rense-watcher. And it worked. 

Circulation and ads rose, along with recognition. But the camaraderie Rense established with her small staff deteriorated as she became a public persona, doing the social minuet, signing up influential socialites as "contributing editors," appearing on TV talk shows. Meanwhile, she went through a painful divorce from Arthur Rense (whom she remarried in 1987). Soon, several former staffers agree, she became distant. There was "an atmosphere of fear," even "terror." Moody and mercurial, she was deemed "tyrannical." New employees were told by colleagues that it wasn't a good idea to keep children's photos on one's desk, because Rense didn't have children; that if she was going to a press party, no one else should; that you shouldn't get in the elevator if she was on it. Dismissing it all, Rense says, "We all have problems with authority figures."

The firings at AD became legendary. A prophetic passage in "Ciao, Sherry!" described a tough office manager "who severed heads quickly, cleanly, without last rites. She just pulled the black hood over her head and chopped." The lines could have been written about AD, from reports of former employees who claim they were axed without warning by personnel, then given a few hours to clear their desks and leave the building. Rense insists that the quick boot was company policy.

No one, however, could argue that the magazine wasn't thriving -- and Rense was the reason. Although many people have toiled for her behind the scenes, doing virtually all the editing and ghost-writing her editor's letter, drafting the copy for her 12 AD books and even, on occasion, autographing them for her, just about everything was her vision, her concept. By 1979, advertising revenues had hit $10.3 million. With 1,158 ad pages that year, AD was getting dangerously close to House & Garden's 1,417. (Ten years later, with 1,889 pages, it had left HG, with its 990 pages, far behind.) 

Reportedly, Rense rejected overtures from Conde Nast and Hearst, preferring to stay at Knapp, where she enjoyed autonomy -- and protected it zealously. Knapp, who calls Rense "domineering," felt her wrath once after bringing in a management consultant: "If I have to answer to him," she stormed, "I'll go across the street and work for Prudential." 

Moonlighting for Knapp, she gave her all to his 1975 acquisition, Bon Appetit, whose masthead still lists her as "founding editor." Although she was opposed to his 1981 acquisition of the American edition of Geo, the glossy German travel-art magazine, she gave it her best shot -- to no avail. The magazine folded in 1985. But Rense was already running out of steam. "I was tired," she says. "I began asking my business manager, 'When can I get out?' "

Rense snapped out of her lethargy in 1983, when Conde Nast rolled out a redesigned House & Garden. Going after AD's upscale audience, the magazine cut its circulation to 660,000 and adopted the portfolio-of-homes approach used by AD. To Rense's fury, the remake won an award from the American Society of Magazine Editors, the industry's highest honor. 

"They were arrogant to steal my format," she says. "It made me mad." Rense counterattacked. In June 1985, AD published a special issue devoted entirely to the English country house. It was a smashing success, and Rense began putting out an annual country house issue. Next came the annual New York issue (November) and an international issue (January). To counter AD's image as nothing more than a picture book, the magazine paid top dollar to recruit writers like John Updike, Margaret Atwood and William Styron. 

Rense was on a roll. Conde Nast, meanwhile, struggled. In 1986, House & Garden's editor, Louis Oliver Gropp, was out. Anna Wintour was brought in from British Vogue to pinch-hit. She swiftly changed the magazine's name to HG and developed an idiosyncratic blend of fashion and interior design. Though probably the wave of the future, it was too much of a mishmash for the stodgy china and crystal advertiser crowd. AD had won both rounds.

Rense kept up the offensive, though. In quick succession she put out a trial spinoff called AD Travels. When it failed as a stand-alone, she stuffed it into the magazine, where advertisers had wanted it all along. Then she introduced regular architecture sections, and in December will bring out an all-architecture theme issue. In April, her Academy Awards Collectors Issue, showing the homes of such Golden Age stars as Charles Chaplin, Mary Pickford, Gloria Swanson, and Gary Cooper, turned out to be the magazine's second-largest newsstand seller ever -- surpassed only by the December 1981 cover of the Reagans' private quarters in the White House.

While the competition obsesses about beating AD at the newsstand, Rense now spends much of her time dreaming up promotional projects to generate miscellaneous revenue. With the magazine industry in recession, AD's advertising will decline slightly in November for the first time in years, and the brains at AD are working overtime to keep their weighty ship on an even keel. In the process, the magazine sometimes appears to obliterate the sacrosanct divide between the business and editorial sides of the enterprise. The traditional magazine "separation of church and state can't work," Bud Knapp explains. "Editors have to be more responsive to marketing."

The responsive Rense came up with the AD 100, a decorators' source guide inspired by the Forbes 400 (or, some critics say, by a decorators' source guide shopped to Knapp Communications by John C. Aves, a Chicago ad man and fishing buddy of Bud Knapp's). Presented to readers as a kind of 13th issue, the AD 100 ruffled feathers by leaving out chintz royals like the New York firm of Parish-Hadley, but it was a major success: its 133 pages of ads will keep AD's 1990 ad figures from falling below last year's. Next year's bonus will be a guide to the top 100 architects, a Machiavellian move that will enlist the support of Rense's most supercilious critics.

Rense's latest brainstorm, and potentially most controversial idea, is the AD Collection, to be unveiled in the December issue. It's a haute mail-order catalogue featuring 26 antiques and works of art priced from $15,000 to $800,000, most of them from AD advertisers. In a kind of twist on the logo-stamped novelties that magazines often peddle in their pages, AD will offer readers not mugs, aprons or calendars, but a pair of rare Adam mirrors, a 17th-century Japanese screen or a Sheridan-style breakfront with palm-frond top.

"Why not give dealers a whole new clientele, and open a world for the reader who may not have a decorator?" Rense rationalizes.  "They can feel confident about what they buy." The dealers pay nothing for the honor of inclusion -- it's not considered advertising. If an item sells, however, the 20 percent commission that would normally go to a decorator (so far, the decorators are simmering in silence) will be split between charity (5 percent) and the magazine (15 percent) -- opening up a whole new source of revenue. "We'll make a nice profit," says Rense, sounding just like the member of the Knapp board she is. (She is also exploring the idea of having AD sell grand house plans, by master architects of the past and present.)

"Leave it to Paige to push the envelope," says an astonished John Mack Carter, president of the American Society of Magazine Editors and editor in chief of Good Housekeeping. As for the ethics involved, he says, "It's not a conflict so long as it is conducted as a service to the reader and not a profit center." Carter pauses. "Paige Rense, merchant -- interesting idea."

That may not be the only surprising change that AD readers see in the 90's. With the lines drawn in the sands of Malibu, the Italian Riviera and the Hamptons, the next decade will be as interesting for how design magazines deal with the new coolness toward conspicuous consumption as for how they compete for houses to publish and for market share.

Many people wonder, as does Nancy Novogrod, editor in chief of the newly resurgent HG, whether "the house as a work of art, perfectly composed, pristine and untouched, isn't old hat now." Paige Rense, den mother to the "$200,000 doesn't go very far" decorator, knows the stuffing is coming out of the excessively rich look -- Knapp's own consumer studies have told her so. So AD will look different -- and in time, so will the taste of its readers. "Paige Rense can't dictate how designers design," Bud Knapp says, "but she influences by what she chooses."

Insiders ask, however, whether Rense's loyalty to designers who stuck with her during the House & Garden wars isn't standing in the way of a fresh look, whether AD wouldn't be better positioned for the 90's with an editor who has fewer political debts. Bud Knapp insists he is in no rush for her to take off her spurs. "I want her to keep working as long as she can type."

When the woman Knapp calls "the keeper of the sacred flame" does go, it won't be with a pile of company stock: other than her employee profit sharing plan, she has no equity in the company that has given her boss a net worth of $200 million. This is a sore subject. "Once, Bud told me all his friends want to know why I get all the publicity," Rense says. "I told him, all my friends want to know why he gets all the money."

But Rense is not talking retirement. Nor does she see AD as king of the hill, invulnerable to attack. In her office, she flounces her blue denim cowgirl skirt, leans forward squarely, and digs her boot heels in the beige wall-to-wall. "I'm still David, not Goliath. Conde Nast and Hearst have billions trained at me. I am outmanned and outmonied." But is she worried? "Oh God, no!" she exclaims, those eyes widening. "They're never going to beat me!"

headline:
The Executive Life;
When Politics and Profits Just Don't Mix
abstract:
TIANANMEN Square. The mere mention of Beijing's biggest public plaza brings back horrific memories of the bloody student uprising that was staged there last year and then quashed by the Chinese Government. Relations between the United States and China have since chilled considerably, and Congress has sought to show its disapproval of the Communist Government's violent crackdown through various diplomatic sanctions.

But American executives have not seemed as inclined to back off from China. I.B.M., Exxon and Mobil Oil are just three of the big American corporations with operations in China, and there are scores of trading companies that do business there.

headline: A Treasure of Kitchen Hand-Me-Downs
abstract:
SHOPS devoted to vintage clothing, 50's furniture, used books or costume jewelry are easy to find. But a shrine to second-hand pots and pans? Meet Judy Kaminsky, the proprietor of Cookin' in San Francisco; it may be the only shop dedicated to used cookware. 

"I have what you can't get anymore," Ms. Kaminsky said of the 20,000 items -- give or take a few hundred -- that fill her large shop in the East Haight district of the city. BLACKBOARD;
Peace Corps Not for Novices
abstract:
LIBERAL arts college students who count the Peace Corps among their postgraduate plansare discovering that it is not a sure bet: they must prepare for the program as carefully as they plan their careers.

Many countries served by the Peace Corps have raised their standards, seeking volunteers with skills tailored to their needs. So these days, prerequisites for liberal arts students include more emphasis on language study, particularly French or Spanish, since many volunteers serve incentral Africa, where French is the dominant language, and Central America. Also stressed are demonstrated leadership abilities and experience as a volunteer or other special requirements, such as first-aid training.

headline:
DINING OUT;
French Fare in a Banksville Farmhouse
abstract:
WORD of a new chef at La Cremaillere inspired our recent revisits to this rustic farmhouse restaurant run with some success since 1962 by "Robert Meyzen, pere et fils," as the father and son owners style themselves. In addition to the work at the stove, we noted several other changes deserving of mention. Lending an oddly modern feel to the old, unpretentious clapboard farmhouse, the entrance addition now provides space for a dramatic indoor staircase massed with plants and seasonal flowers. 

 Inside, the first room, once the antechamber, retains shelves displaying an attractive collection of provincial china but has been put to good dining use. It is now the most pleasant of La Cremaillere's dining rooms. Tables are spaced at easy intervals and ventilation is excellent, both amenities missing in the older areas; and a pretty country print drapes the windows and covers the shades of sconces giving off a golden glow.

headline:
WINTER IN THE SUN;
1492 and All That: Island Events
abstract:
IN 1492 Christopher Columbus, stubbornly seeking a sea route to China but landing instead on the islands of the Caribbean, thought he had found the mythical Isles of the Blest. While the consequences of that error-ridden voyage are still everywhere palpable in daily life on both sides of the Atlantic, the quincentennial anniversary next year will serve as an occasion for a host of commemorations, celebrations and observances throughout the Caribbean that specifically invoke the spirit of The Discoverer.

The waters of the Caribbean will be crowded with regattas of reproductions of caravels and private boats attempting to trace Columbus's voyage from his sketchy and often intentionally misleading logs. Among others, a crew of Japanese sailors aboard a copy of the Santa Maria will fulfill Columbus's original goal of reaching the East -- though with the help of the Panama Canal -- by sailing from Barcelona to Kobe, Japan, touring the Caribbean along the way.

headline: Hong Kong Defies Its Bosses
abstract:
The normally tame legislature of this British colony has staged an unprecedented revolt by rejecting an accord reached by Britain and China. The revolt reflects a sense of betrayal felt by Hong Kong residents, who are not being consulted by those deciding their fate. They fear that when China takes over the colony in 1997, the world will consider what China does here an internal affair, as in Tibet. They need American support.

The revolt took place over the composition of a Court of Final Appeal, a supreme court. The court would succeed the Privy Council in London. On Dec. 5, the day after the Legislative Council rejected the model for the court that Britain and China had agreed upon, China said Hong Kong had no right to repudiate the accord.

headline: A Chinese Master
abstract:
To anyone who thinks China is moist green paddy and bamboo groves, Shaanxi can seem another country: arid, austere, pale with wheat and yellow earth. Yet it is the Chinese heartland, famous as the province where the first Emperor of China was buried with his vast terra-cotta army and where the Communists' epic Long March ended. It is also where Zhang Yimou, China's most accomplished film director, was born and where he is shooting his new movie, "The Story of Qiuju." 

Winter here is three-toned: the white slopes, the brown earth, the gray fingers of bare poplars. And brightness strikes only around the set -- the redness of chilies hanging from the eaves of a farmhouse. Lashings of red tint Zhang's pictures. "No color," he has said, "is more redolent of China."

headline:
DINING OUT;
Shanghai Cuisine Arrives in Larchmont
abstract:
AVOIDING the doldrums in which the once unique Hunan-Sichuan cuisine has been mired -- in most Chinese restaurants the style is now a catchword for whatever the kitchen feels like turning out that's hot with red chili -- Ray's Cafe comes to our rescue. Since it opened seven months ago, this tiny place has attracted a growing clientele delighted with the subtle, ultra-light versions of Shanghai cooking, the cuisine already known for its fresh tastes and natural flavors.

Because of its nearness to many lakes, the marshy land of the Yangtze Delta and the China Sea, the coastal area around Shanghai has been called the land of fish and rice. And diners will find rice in many forms figuring prominently in this cuisine -- in rice noodles, rice wine and rice vinegar, the last two often used as a replacement for soy sauce or salt.

headline: Taking On Mount Kinabalu
abstract:
KINABALU is no mountain for old men. Towering 13,455 feet over the jungles of north Borneo, it is the highest peak in Southeast Asia. But I feel no hesitation, no self-doubt, despite my 43 years. The path is groomed to the top, and when I last hiked to comparable heights -- although it was 10 years ago -- I suffered nothing more than sunburn.

 My wife is perfectly content to stay below, snug in the lavish confines of the Tanjung Aru Beach Hotel, a getaway for expatriates, business executives and other travelers to East Malaysia. There's a pool shimmering before us like a heated oasis. But there's also the mountain, 60 miles into the interior, and I feel its shadow.

headline: A Cultural Exchange at Long Wharf
abstract:
"THE most important and demanding thing is to keep freshness in your work," said Arvin Brown, artistic director of Long Wharf Theater. "I may fall on my face. But what makes me enjoy what I do is that I'm still always tackling something new. In the creative arts, to stand still is to go backward."

Twenty-five years ago, just out of the Yale School of Drama, Mr. Brown assumed artistic command of the newly hatched theater in New Haven. Since then, Hal Holbrook, Joanne Woodward, Jason Robards and many other stars have performed there, and more than 20 plays have moved from Long Wharf to Off Broadway and Broadway, garnering Pulitzers and Tonys along their way.

headline: Resettled Tibetans Are Anxious to Leave Politics, Not Culture, Behind
abstract:
LATER this month six Tibetan men and women who have lived in exile in India or Nepal will migrate to Connecticut, settling into homes and jobs that are being offered nationwide to 1,000 exiled Tibetans. It is such a small number, no more than 25 are expected in the state during the next year. But to Dicki Gyamcho, who is coordinating the project in Connecticut, the arrival of the Tibetans adds a personal link to a chain of events that began in 1959, a decade after the Chinese had invaded their homeland.

That year, a young Tibetan woman journeyed by pickup truck across the Himalayas into India. Her husband followed the same route several months later. They were among 100,000 Tibetans who fled as the Chinese Government attempted to destroy Tibet. The exodus was led by their political and spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, who set up a government in India, conceding that freedom was possible only in exile.

headline: The Next Revolution
abstract:
I am back in China and I have found a China that the outside world does not know about. For three years, I have yearned to return to the land of my birth. I was forced to flee after the bloody confrontation between tanks and people. I have come back to touch, taste and smell the wonders of this beautiful place. headline: The Torturers of Lingyuan
abstract:
In the early evening of April 22, 1991, a prison van left the Great North Prison in Shenyang, carrying 11 political prisoners who were convicted for their part in the pro-democracy movement. Among them were Liu Gang, a physicist, and Zhang Ming, an engineer -- Beijing student leaders on the most-wanted list -- and Tang Yuanjuan, also an engineer. They were sent to the Lingyuan No. 2 Labor Reform Detachment in Liaoning Province, known to the outside world as the Lingyuan Motor Vehicle General Assembly Plant. It makes Linghe tractors and trucks under the brand name Huanghe (Yellow River).

From April 22 to May 29, the authorities gave them an "orientation course," requiring the prisoners to recite from memory the "standards of conduct for criminals undergoing reform" -- in essence, a way to instill "criminal consciousness" into them. Liu Gang and 10 other new political prisoners refused to take the memory test. Liu Gang and five others were shackled with leg irons and thrown either into solitary confinement or a strict regime unit. The other five were allowed to stay in the brigade to be "corrected." For days, the authorities tried to break their spirits. The inmates went on a hunger strike to protest the brutality, only making conditions worse.
