abstract:
AN antiquing tour through Kentucky Bluegrass Country -- an enticing area of horse farms and small towns surrounding Lexington -- means a chance to unearth some great buys in American antiques and, in the bargain, enjoy some of the most beautiful rural countryside anywhere.

The route my wife, Ruth, and I chose last summer began in Lexington, which has plenty of good hotels and motels, and then took in a dozen "down home" towns that are particularly good for antiques. We went from Berea and Lancaster to Frankfort, Paris and Winchester -- all within a circle only 60 miles across. Some of the towns lie along smaller routes and side roads, such as Midway on U.S. Route 62 and Paris on U.S. 68, which afford picturesque views of the horse farms.

No Such Thing as Free Radio
abstract:
President Clinton is right to propose that the Government's international broadcasting operations be consolidated. Merging Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty with the Voice of America would end duplication, save money and create a more effective service. Consolidation would prove that the Government is serious about undertaking the restructuring long under way in the private sector.

Speaking for myself and not for the V.O.A., there is no longer a need for two taxpayer-financed international broadcasting services; the collapse of Communism has seen to that. The Voice of America, based in Washington, broadcasts worldwide in 50 languages. Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty broadcast from Munich in two dozen languages to post-Communist Europe and the former Soviet Union. Each service costs more than $220 million a year.

headline: Germany's Island Fortresses
abstract:
"EVERYTHING here is so settled that one knows exactly everybody's station and standing." So wrote Annette von Droste-Hulshoff, Germany's pre-eminent 19th-century poet, nearly 160 years ago about the Munsterland. She was born and spent most of her life there in largely self-imposed literary seclusion composing ballads and novellas.

Today her portrait is in millions of wallets on the backside of 20-mark banknotes, and it still seems as if nothing has changed in Munsterland, a small Delaware-sized area on the North German Plain between the Dutch border and the bustling coal-mining, steel-making Ruhr Basin.

headline: A Guide to Guidebooks For Who You Are, Not Where You're Going
abstract:
AS anyone who has ever stayed at the Casablanca Holiday Inn will know, the difference between a traveler and a tourist lies not in the place visited but in the process employed, not in where you go but how. You can be a traveler in Paris -- that most touristy of cities -- if somehow you break through the surface of the cafe and get invited for Sunday dinner with your waiter's family. The distinction has nothing to do with going, as some people have suggested, to a place that can't be found in any guidebook; rather, it implies going without one.

Which, as we suspected all along, makes the great majority of us tourists. Rare, I think, is the travel writer who doesn't use a guidebook, and even rarer is the travel writer who admits that he does. An exception is the English journalist Richard West who, looking for a place to stay in Granada, Nicaragua, in the mid-1980's ("Hurricane in Nicaragua: A Journey in Search of Revolution"), turned to the "South American Handbook," "that legendary guide that every serious traveler, including Graham Greene, carries about with him in this part of the world." The Travelers World Guide series editors reciprocated in their "Mexico and Central American Handbook" by noting that Belize City's Old Louisville Democratic Bar was recommended by Mr. West. But most writers give the impression that they are above the mundane concerns of cheap hotels and are traveling in an altogether higher, and more trailblazing, sphere. If they mention books at all, they are usually novels, the more incongruous the setting the better. Greene, in this part of the world, talked not of handbooks but of Trollope.

headline:
The View From: New Haven;
How Children's Art Creates Diversions for Hospitalized Children
abstract:
NO scientific evidence exists that art heals, the chief of pediatrics at Yale-New Haven Hospital, Dr. Joseph B. Warshaw, said. "I can't give you data that looking at a picture makes a kid get better faster," he said, "but it sure makes them feel better." Sick children will be able to look at hundreds of art works from many nations at the new children's hospital in New Haven, which will begin accepting young patients this month.

 "Tales of Courage" is the name of the art program begun last year to decorate the walls and halls of the new hospital with an international collection of children's art. Participants from 4 to 18 years old could choose as their theme, acts or words of courage, faces or symbols of courage. Each child prepared a visual piece and wrote a short statement or poem on the theme of courage. Pieces grouped on one of the atrium walls will serve as the children's art gallery.

headline: A Coldblooded Cure
abstract:
AS A MEDICAL TEAM PREPARES FOR openheart surgery, the starkly furnished operating room in Siberia is eerily quiet. It takes a moment to figure out: the beeping of monitors, so familiar to Western ears, is absent. There is no heart-lung machine to reroute the 12-year-old patient's blood. Instead, doctors have packed the body in ice to block the flow of blood to brain, and stopped the heart with potassium chloride. They have rendered her clinically dead.

The surgeons have only 90 minutes to repair the hole in the child's heart without risking brain damage. As the last stitch is placed, they pour a pitcher of warm water over the heart, pump it with their hands and administer dopamine to restore its function. Relief fills the room as her temperature creeps up from 72 degrees. Over the next three days she will thaw out and wake up.

headline: Connecticut's Link to Salvaging Artifacts From the Titanic
abstract:
THE oldest living survivor of the Titanic, 97-year-old Edith Haisman, of Southampton, England, says she never expected to get another look at the gold pocket watch that went down to the bottom of the sea with her father when the ocean liner struck an iceberg and sank off the coast of Newfoundland during its maiden voyage nearly 82 years ago.

But last December, a Connecticut corporation intent on establishing a Titanic museum gave Mrs. Haisman a watch it said was her father's. The corporation, R.M.S. Titanic Inc., with offices in Southport and Manhattan, says it can earn more than $100 million during a 10-year world tour by featuring relics salvaged from a debris field near the wreckage.

headline: Learning To Stand On Ceremony
abstract:
Sondra Snowdon's first lesson in international business diplomacy and global social protocol came in 1982 when, as a liaison for Citicorp, she was sent to meet a sheik at the airport and he assumed that she was his gift for the weekend. It took her quite a while to convince him that she was not a gift, and when she finally did, it was she who had to apologize so as not to offend.

Today, Ms. Snowdon markets that and other protocol lessons by way of Snowdon's Global Trade and Travel Network, an on-line computer data base that provides global-minded executives a comprehensive protocol-oriented overview of 64 countries. She also offers a worldwide business briefing service by fax and has written two books on the subject (her second, "Snowdon's Official International Protocols," will be published in September by Irwin Professional Publishers). And she does seminars; in annual sessions at the Pierre Hotel she teaches the staff the intricacies of dealing with Japanese guests.

headline: Celebrating A Passion For Roses
abstract:
IT IS almost always worth the trip to visit a collection founded on passion. The passion of Jules Gravereaux, a late 19th-century millionaire and co-founder of the stylish Bon Marche department store in Paris, was for roses -- and it led to the creation in 1894 of the first garden in Europe designed exclusively for them: La Roseraie Departementale de l'Hay-les-Roses, 20 minutes south of Paris by car or 40 minutes by Metro and bus. Not too long after, in 1904, Mr. Gravereaux donated 6,000 roses from l'Hay to the city of Paris to start the rose garden at Bagatelle in the Bois de Boulogne, the city's vast park of over 2,000 acres. The Bagatelle, an 18th century house surrounded by extensive gardens, includes the sumptuous two-acre rose garden. Planted with 11,000 rosebushes of over 850 varieties, it is in bloom throughout the summer.

Mr. Gravereaux and J. C. N. Forestier, the conservator of parks and gardens of Paris and the landscape architect who designed and executed the garden, aimed to put Bagatelle on a par with the best rose gardens of England and Germany and hoped that it would be of general interest to everyone "from the most modest amateur to the most qualified rose specialists," as Mr. Gravereaux wrote.

headline: Glen Cove Artist With a Passion for Mongolian Paintings
abstract:
MOU-SIEN TSENG made his first impassioned Mongolian man-and-horse paintings with white chalk on a sidewalk when he was 5. 

Fifty-two years later Mou-Sien, now living in Glen Cove, is still deeply involved with painting scenes from Mongolian life. Only now the artist pours his passion into detailed acrylic paintings on large gold-and-silver-leaf canvases, garnering international recognition and praise for his bold renditions -- with sometimes radical departures -- from traditional interpretations of the Mongolian man-and-horse motif.

headline:
REDISCOVERIES;
More Than Just A Victorian
abstract:
Three-quarters of a century have slipped away since Bloomsbury last sneered at the British Victorians; fiction's new career, in the form of "Ulysses," began more than 70 years ago. We post-moderns are by now so far from the modernist repudiation of Victorian influence that we can look with an unembarrassed eye -- an eye of one's own, we might say -- at the three-decker Victorian novel's subplots and coincidences, its bloated serializations, its unnaturally heightened and speechifying dialogue. We can see past their potboiler mechanisms into what these baggy old novelists humanly, and sometimes half-divinely, knew.

Anthony Trollope has long been excluded from this percipient, and undeceived, reassessment. He is nearly the only Victorian novelist who has been critically doomed to remain a Victorian. He alone appears to be unforgiven. Dickens and Henry James and George Eliot and Thackeray -- even the colonialist-imperialist Kipling! -- are permitted, and sometimes prodded, to transcend the accident of their chronology and the confines of their mores. Only Trollope is regarded as still mired in his devices -- devices that are, in their pre-video yet cinematic way, archetypes of our present-day story-machines, glowing like colored apothecary globes in rooms where pianos used to stand. Trollope, in brief, is dismissed as a kind of antiquated television set; he is said to be "undemanding." Dickens, by contrast, survives in all his greatness as caricaturist; George Eliot as moralist; Thackeray as ironist; Hardy as determinist. (Shorthand, it goes without saying, for the orchestrally manifold.)

headline: Yeltsin's Next Quagmire?
abstract:
Unlike Russia's secessionist crisis in Chechnya, the danger of a collapse of Tajikistan peace talks and renewal of the civil war there-- by far the bloodiest in any of the former Soviet republics -- cannot be dismissed as an internal Russian matter.

United States policy should aim to develop the small Central Asian republic of Tajikistan as an independent member of the world community. Instead, Washington has been surprisingly silent from the time war broke out in May 1992 until a cease-fire took hold in October in the small mountain country of 5.6 million, sandwiched between Afghanistan, China, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan.

headline: A Soaring Fund Shuns Japan and Mexico
abstract:
Spectacular market losses in currency-battered Mexico and quake-shaken Japan have decimated many a foreign fund in recent months. Standing tall is GAM International.

 Its manager, John R. Horseman, adroitly dodged the danger zones, kept a significant cash cushion and larded his portfolio with European bonds, especially German ones. For the year, he has logged a total return of more than 9 percent, well ahead of the 7 percent loss for the average foreign stock fund. Although the surge follows a weak showing in 1994, his long-term record is stellar. For the five years ended in February, GAM International's annualized return exceeded 14 percent, adjusted for its 5 percent sales charge.

headline: WEEKEND GETAWAYS; Newport's Great Indoors
abstract:
NARRAGANSETT BAY glowed cornflower blue as I crossed the bridge to Newport, R.I., one windy April weekend. In summer, the city is a mecca for sailors and swimmers, but because it was too early to enjoy the beaches and ocean, I would be exploring Newport indoors before the crowds arrived. 

 I had made reservations at the Sanford-Covell Villa Marina, a three-story stick style house with a decorative arts interior on Narragansett Bay in the gaslighted colonial Point neighborhood, less than a mile from the center of town. The house, on the National Register of Historic Places, has a magnificent three-story entryway, open from floor to ceiling and stenciled in floral and geometric designs. The bayside parlor contained two baby grand pianos and crystal decanters of port and sherry. I felt comfortable right away, as if I were visiting my grandmother's house -- if my grandmother had been rich.

abstract: China's government will try 38 suspects in hijacking of ship in 1998, suggesting that it may be cracking down on high-seas piracy; release of suspected pirates several times in recent years noted (S)

headline: Portugal Lowers Its Flag, Handing Macao to China
abstract: Portugal relinquishes Macao to China, ending 442 years of colonial rule and shaking off the last vestiges of European colonial influence in Asia; police break up gathering of members of the Falun Gong spiritual movement; first contingent of Chinese troops crosses the border; photos; map (M)

headline: Chinese Tire Maker Sues Goodyear
abstract: Goodyear Tire and Rubber Co is sued by China Tire Holdings, which accuses Goodyear of lavishing gifts on Chinese officials to secure interest in tire plant; China Tire says Goodyear interfered with its own interests in Dalian, China, plant and violated several US laws, including one barring payments intended to influence foreign officials; suit is seeking $3.5 billion (S)
